idiom_name: consumer-defined interface plus a struct holding *sql.DB (database/sql)
implementation_notes: Go has no classes and does not need them for this pattern: the DAO is a small interface declared next to its consumer plus a struct holding a *sql.DB handle, because the standard library already owns connection pooling, context-based cancellation and statement execution, leaving the DAO only the SQL and the Scan-to-struct mapping. What replaces the classic structure is implicit interface satisfaction: the concrete type satisfies the interface without registering anywhere, and dependency injection replaces the DAO factory, so a second store is simply a second type. Keep the interface small and in domain terms; when each aggregate has its own method set, a concrete struct without an interface is the honest minimum.
pitfalls: Rows must be closed and checked: without defer rows.Close() the pool leaks connections, and without rows.Err() a mid-iteration failure looks like a short result set.
Declaring the DAO interface next to the implementation instead of the consumer produces bloated interfaces; the Go convention is a small interface where it is used, satisfied implicitly.
Wrapping store errors carelessly breaks errors.Is/errors.As; keep the sentinels reachable (wrap sql.ErrNoRows) instead of comparing error strings.

variants.name: Generic DAO[T] with a per-entity scan hook (Go generics)
variants.idiom_name: DAO[T any] over *sql.DB with a scan func(*sql.Rows) (T, error)
variants.implementation_notes: Type parameters remove the duplication the pattern is usually criticised for: one generic DAO[T] parameterised by the entity type plus a per-type hook (table name and scan function) implements the shared CRUD once, while entity-specific queries stay as extra methods on a thin wrapper around it. Choose it when many aggregates genuinely share the same CRUD shape; keep the plain interface when each aggregate has its own method set, because generics add a layer of indirection without deleting real duplication.
pitfalls: The table name is string-concatenated into SQL: it must come from a compile-time allow-list, never from user input, because generics provide no safety there.
A generic DAO looks type-safe while the scan hook still hides column-to-field mapping errors; keep one hook per entity and test it against the real schema.
